name: Intraocular Pressure
remarks: Submodule for IOP procedure and findings with expanded medications, glaucoma diagnosis, and follow-up care.
IOP is attribute-driven and persistent across visits (`iop_reading`). The Observation state class
has no `assign_to_attribute` field -- only `attribute` -- so a JSON module that sets
`assign_to_attribute` on an Observation is silently ignored by the engine; the value must instead
be drawn by a SetAttribute state and read back into the Observation via its real `attribute` field.
A tier is drawn once per patient (Baseline_Tier_Roll). On every later visit the reading is
redrawn within a narrow band keyed off treatment status and that tier (Elevated_IOP_Jitter /
Normal_IOP_Jitter / Treated_IOP_Jitter), instead of a fresh independent 8-35 mmHg roll every
visit. The original per-visit design OR-combined two independent 8-35 draws
(P(either eye > 21) = 1-(1-14/27)^2 = 0.77), flagging ~77% of visits as elevated and making
nearly every recurring patient (e.g. every T2 diabetic routed through this submodule)
glaucomatous over time. Both eyes' Observations read the same persisted value; per-eye divergence
was not modelled, keeping the attribute contract to a single shared `iop_reading`.
Fix round 1 (reviewer finding): the first version of this fix replaced the per-visit re-roll
with a persistent tier, but derived the tier from a Draw_Baseline_IOP Uniform(8,35) split at 21
-- (35-21)/(35-8) = 51.9% of patients landed in the elevated tier, and Elevated_IOP_Jitter's
Uniform(22,32) was entirely above the 21 threshold, so elevation was deterministic every visit
once tiered. The reviewer's 200k-patient Monte Carlo measured ~50% of patients acquiring a
lifetime glaucoma (~7.5%) or OHT (~42.7%) diagnosis by visit 2 -- against a real combined
glaucoma+OHT prevalence of roughly 10-15% in an older/diabetic ophthalmology-clinic population
(POAG prevalence ~2-2.5% in US adults 40+ rising sharply with age past 70 [Vajaranant et al.,
NHANES-based estimates]; OHT prevalence ~3-6% in population surveys [Beaver Dam Eye Study,
Baltimore Eye Survey]; diabetes carries an independently elevated open-angle-glaucoma risk in
several cohort/meta-analyses [e.g. Zhou et al. 2014] -- composited to the 10-15% figure used
here, not a single precise source). Fixed two ways:
- Baseline_Tier_Roll now assigns the tier directly from a sourced 15%/85% weighted split
(distributed_transition) instead of deriving it from a uniform numeric draw.
- Elevated_IOP_Jitter's band was widened to Uniform(15,33) so it straddles the 21 mmHg
threshold (P(>21) = 12/18 = 66.7% per visit) instead of guaranteeing elevation every time --
representing real IOP's visit-to-visit and diurnal variability, and giving OHT/glaucoma a
non-zero chance of going undetected on any single visit.
With those two numbers: P(diagnosed by visit 1 | elevated tier) = 0.667, population-wide
0.15*0.667 = 10.0%. P(diagnosed by visit 2) = 1-(1-0.667)^2 = 0.889, population-wide
0.15*0.889 = 13.3%. As visits -> infinity this converges to the tier fraction itself, 15.0%
-- so the combined lifetime-diagnosis rate is bracketed within the target 10-15% band across
the whole realistic range of follow-up length (10.0% at first exposure, 15.0% as an upper
asymptote), not just at one arbitrarily chosen visit count. Within a qualifying reading,
P(>30 | >21) = (3/18)/(12/18) = 25%, so of eventual diagnoses roughly 1-in-4 land in the
glaucoma band (>30) and 3-in-4 in the OHT band (21-30) -- population-wide asymptotically
~3.75% glaucoma / ~11.25% OHT, a plausible ratio (OHT is more prevalent than diagnosed
glaucoma in the underlying population literature cited above).
Diagnosis (Glaucoma_Diagnosis / Ocular_Hypertension_Diagnosis) and medication ordering are each
attribute-guarded so a patient already carrying the diagnosis, or already on a drop, is not
re-diagnosed or re-ordered on every subsequent visit. Glaucoma drops are chronic:true, matching
real-world indefinite once-daily/twice-daily dosing rather than a one-time fill.
Two RxNorm codes were wrong and have been replaced with RxNav-verified SCDs (Semantic Clinical
Drugs; the previous codes were an SCDC and a bare ingredient, neither a dispensable drug):
- brimonidine: RxCUI 1999015 (previously used here) is an SCDC, "brimonidine tartrate 0.25
MG/ML" -- an ingredient+strength component with no dose form, and its strength did not even
match this state's own display text. Replaced with RxCUI 861204, the SCD "brimonidine tartrate
1 MG/ML Ophthalmic Solution" (verified via RxNav rxcui/861204/historystatus). This is also the
exact code eye/ophthalmic_progression.json's treatment-detection check looks for, so ordering it
here now closes that IOP feedback loop instead of the two modules silently disagreeing.
- timolol: RxCUI 10600 was an IN (ingredient-only "timolol", no strength or dose form).
Replaced with RxCUI 2702393, the SCD "timolol hemihydrate 5 MG/ML Ophthalmic Solution"
(verified via RxNav), the closest unqualified (non-preservative-free, non-extended-release)
generic match to the original display text; RxNorm has no plain "timolol maleate ... ophthalmic
solution" SCD as of this writing.
First visit for this patient (iop_reading unset) rolls a fresh population tier;
every later visit re-enters here and only jitters the existing reading.
One-time population tier assignment, 15% elevated / 85% normal -- a sourced weight (see
module remarks for the combined glaucoma+OHT prevalence citation), not derived from a
numeric draw. The tier persists (iop_baseline_tier) across all future visits until treated.

remarks: Controlled range on therapy, reflecting the ~25-30% IOP reduction typical of prostaglandin
analog / beta-blocker / CAI monotherapy.
Straddles the 21 mmHg elevated threshold (P(>21) = 12/18 = 66.7% per visit) instead of the
old Uniform(22,32), which was entirely above it and so guaranteed an elevated reading, and
therefore an eventual diagnosis, on every single visit. See module remarks for the resulting
population-wide diagnosis-rate arithmetic.
Normal IOP range is 10-21 mmHg, but can be higher in pathological conditions
